extracted.intended_audience: intellectual property practitioners, patent examiners, policymakers, and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether claimed inventions (especially processes) meet U.S. patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, based on Diamond v. Diehr: definition of 'process', the transformation test, whole-claim evaluation, and how abstract elements (algorithms, laws of nature, computer implementation) affect eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'process' under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'process' is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result; if new and useful, it is just as patentable as a piece of machinery (Cochrane v. Deener).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Cochrane/Deener formulation: processes are methods of treating materials to produce a result. The 1952 Act's use of 'process' was intended broadly ('include anything under the sun that is made by men'). When evaluating claims described as processes, treat them as methods of treatment producing a result rather than dismissing them because they are not a machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation and reduction (machine-or-transformation) test
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Transformation and reduction of an article "to a different state or thing" is the clue to the patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed process effects a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (e.g., curing rubber to a new physical state). If the process performs such a transformative function, that supports §101 eligibility. Use transformation as a decisive indicator when a process claim lacks particular machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole-claim evaluation (no analytic dissection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' in judging whether they represent patentable subject matter rather than being dissected into their various elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not strip out or isolate an abstract element (e.g., a mathematical formula) and treat it alone; evaluate the claim's overall character and functionality. Old or known elements included in a claim do not necessarily render the claim unpatentable if the combination as a whole performs a function the patent laws were designed to protect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract formula / law of nature within a process does not automatically defeat eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A process 'is not unpatentable because it contains a law of nature or a mathematical algorithm.' The presence of an abstract formula in a claim does not by itself make the claim ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a mathematical algorithm or law of nature is embedded in a process claim, determine whether the claim as a whole applies the algorithm to produce a practical application (e.g., transforms an article). Mere inclusion of the formula is permissible if the overall process falls within patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer implementation alone does not render a claim unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to subject matter otherwise patentable does not become non-patentable because a computer is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not categorically reject claims solely because they use a computer to perform calculations or control steps. Instead, assess whether the computer-implemented claim, as a whole, performs a patent-eligible function (e.g., contributes to a transformation or practical application) and does not merely preempt an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility focus distinct from novelty/non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an invention falls under patentable subject matter (§101) is a separate inquiry from whether it meets the 'novelty' (§102) or 'non-obviousness' (§103) requirements; those criteria are considered later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining subject-matter eligibility, do not resolve eligibility by reference to novelty or obviousness. First ask whether the claimed subject matter fits within §101 categories (as a whole); only after eligibility is established should novelty and inventive-step analyses be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid preemption of abstract ideas (limitation on software/business-method patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Software-related inventions or business models can be patentable when 'embedded in a proper claim' and do not preempt abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and evaluate claims so they apply an idea to a specific practical application or transformative process rather than claiming the abstract idea itself. Ensure claims are limited to particular implementations or applications that avoid monopolizing the abstract idea across all uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example of allowable claim structure: process applying a formula within an industrial curing operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diamond v. Diehr upheld a claim for a process of molding and curing synthetic rubber that constantly measured temperature inside a mold and fed data into a computer using an existing equation to calculate optimal cure time—i.e., a process applying a formula within an industrial transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such factual patterns as a guide: claims that incorporate measurements, data processing, and application of equations to control a physical, transformative process (e.g., curing a material) illustrate how an abstract formula can be part of a patent-eligible process when the overall claim effects a physical transformation.
